BBC News — published 2026-09-29T19:54:07Z, confirmed from article metadata. Search highlights.
"How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail?"
Counter-terrorism detectives say NO EXPLOSIVES were found in the three vans, only an "accelerant" - petrol. Military remote-controlled robots found no explosives.
The men were held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (PACE), not the Terrorism Act (TACT), which meant detectives had the option of police bail with strict conditions but could not hold the men for 14 days.
Five men from London in their 20s were found parked up near the air base in the middle of the night in suspicious circumstances with some petrol, but "little other usable concrete evidence".
Taylor said the response on Sunday morning was "due to a range of information that we received". Security had been visibly stepped up at the base in the preceding days.
Both counter-terrorism and military sources told the BBC this story is "still quite near the beginning", raising the possibility detectives are trying to identify a "controlling hand" behind the suspects' presence in Whelford with their petrol. Detectives are examining mobile phones and computers, tracking vehicles, searching addresses and using covert techniques of MI5, GCHQ and US intelligence. On that investigation rests whether to arrest anyone else, whether to charge the five, and whether the true story emerges.
Taylor also defended the decision to bail with "very strict conditions", which had been criticised by President Trump.
